report:
## Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by evidence

The claim that abaloparatide reduces vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis is **strongly supported** by high-quality clinical trial evidence.

**Pivotal Trial Evidence:** The ACTIVE trial (Abaloparatide Comparator Trial In Vertebral Endpoints), a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that subcutaneous abaloparatide significantly reduced new vertebral fractures compared with placebo over 18 months. This was published in JAMA, a highly credible peer-reviewed source ([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640); [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/)). The trial also showed reductions in nonvertebral fractures.

**Long-term Extension Data:** Follow-up analysis through the ACTIVE-ACTIVExtend study (43 months total) confirmed that fracture risk reductions and bone mineral density gains persisted across multiple prespecified risk subgroups, reinforcing the durability of the effect ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916366](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916366/)).

**Regulatory Confirmation:** The FDA-approved drug label for TYMLOS (abaloparatide) explicitly states that the drug reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women, based on ACTIVE trial data, with consistent effects regardless of age, years since menopause, prior fracture history, or baseline bone mineral density ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf)).

**Overall Assessment:** This evidence comes from a well-designed randomized controlled trial with regulatory-grade oversight, published in a top-tier journal, with results confirmed by FDA review and extended by long-term follow-up data. The consistency across independent analyses (trial publication, extension studies, and regulatory label) supports high confidence in this claim.
